newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium reveals glimpse of world financial crime.
newsitem.headline: Belgium reveals glimpse of world financial crime.

text.p: Belgium's financial crime taskforce on Tuesday offered a brief glimpse of how the international underworld works.

In a statistical snapshot of 151 cases opened between 1994 and 1996, the Central Office in the Fight Against Economic and Organised Financial Crime presented an inventory of money laundering, drug trafficking, arms smuggling, murder and other crimes estimated to have earned their perpetrators more than 148 billion Belgian francs ($4.2 billion).
It suggested a number of ways on how the fight against crime in Belgium and fraud involving the Brussels-based European Union institutions could be stepped up.

Taskforce director Jean-Pierre Doraene told a news conference that most of its cases involved attempts by drugs gangs based in the Netherlands to launder money through Belgian banks and bureaux de change, mainly in the capital of Brussels.

One case in February 1997 involving a Pakistani man assuming three separate identities had allowed the taskforce to link an unsolved case from 1994, in which a total 6.6 billion francs was laundered at a bureau de change over a period of one month.
In a separate case a Netherlands-based gang had been able to exchange a total 2.5 billion francs in a six-month period in 1996, using five couriers.
Most of the money laundering was carried out by Moroccan, Pakistani or Egyptian nationals, many of whom were not previously known to the police, Doraene said.

The taskforce had also probed international crime, including two cases of terrorism -- one of which was linked to Japan's Aum Shinri Kyo sect, accused of masterminding the 1995 nerve gas attacks on Tokyo's metro system.
Belgian officers had been involved in smashing a fiscal and customs fraud masterminded by an Asian triad gang.
"We have showed that a service like ours is justified," Doraene said.
He said the unit could do more if it was properly staffed and funded and Belgium adopted new legislation on money laundering and organised crime.
The taskforce's budget was so tight its nine investigators had to pay their own mobile phone bills. "It's totally unacceptable," Doraene said.

Between 1994 and 1996 the unit had 1.25 million Belgian francs to spend on new equipment. During the same period it helped seize more than 10 billion francs worth of drugs and illegal funds and property, both in Belgium and abroad.
Doraene said the unit needed to be doubled in size to enable it to do its job better, especially in the area of tax fraud.
Belgium is presently being shaken by allegations of tax fraud organised by banks and involving institutions in Luxembourg.
But the taskforce also praised tax fraud laws in Luxembourg and Switzerland, which it said were better worded than Belgium's own laws.

Cooperation with the European Union's fraud squad, known as UCLAF, could be improved. Belgium treated seven cases involving EU funds between 1994 and 1996 involving around 913 million francs, the taskforce said.
